title: Passkeys move security closer to how people actually live
excerpt: A practical guide to phishing-resistant sign-in, safer account recovery, and the human habits that still matter after passwords begin to disappear.

sections.label: The change
sections.title: A passkey is not just a shorter password.
paragraphs: Passwords ask people to create a secret, remember it, type it into the right site, and recognize every convincing imitation of that site. That is a fragile chain. A passkey changes the mechanism: the service keeps a public key, while the matching private key remains under the user’s control on a device or credential provider.

During sign-in, the credential is scoped to the real service. There is no reusable password for a fake page to collect. The device may ask for a fingerprint, face scan, or PIN, but that local check unlocks the credential; the biometric itself is not sent to the website. This is why WebAuthn-based passkeys are designed to resist phishing and credential replay.

sections.label: Where to start
sections.title: Protect the accounts that can reset everything else.
paragraphs: Begin with the email account, password manager, primary device account, financial accounts, and any administrator or developer identity. These accounts sit at the centre of other recovery paths. Improving a low-value login while leaving the main mailbox exposed does not change the larger risk very much.

Add a passkey from the service’s security settings, test it in a normal sign-in flow, and keep the existing second factor until recovery has also been reviewed. If a service does not support passkeys, use a unique password generated by a password manager and turn on the strongest multi-factor option it offers. One-time codes are still useful, but a code can be relayed to a convincing phishing site; a properly implemented passkey cannot be used for the wrong site.
points: Secure the primary email account first.
Create passkeys only from the real app or a bookmarked, verified domain.
Keep device software, browsers, and credential providers updated.
Remove old devices and unknown sessions from important accounts.
Never approve a sign-in prompt you did not initiate.

sections.label: Recovery
sections.title: The side door must be as strong as the front door.
paragraphs: A secure sign-in can be undermined by weak account recovery. Before relying on a passkey, learn where it is stored, whether it syncs across trusted devices, and what happens if every device is lost. Recovery may use another signed-in device, a hardware security key, carefully stored recovery codes, or a provider’s verified recovery process.

Do not keep the only recovery code on the phone it is meant to recover. Store an offline copy in a protected place, and consider a second hardware-backed credential for accounts whose loss would be severe. Also review the recovery email and phone number: an abandoned address or reassigned number can become an attacker’s route back in.

links.label: FIDO guidance on passkeys and account recovery

sections.label: Shared and public devices
sections.title: Convenience needs a boundary.
paragraphs: A personal device with screen lock and encryption is a reasonable home for a synced passkey. A shared household computer, borrowed phone, school lab, or public terminal is different. Prefer a cross-device sign-in that uses your nearby trusted device, and do not save a credential permanently on hardware you do not control.

For teams, avoid sharing one person’s passkey or account. Give each person an individual identity, use role-based access, and keep an audited emergency account for continuity. Security improves when access can be removed without changing a secret for everyone.

sections.label: A 20-minute upgrade
sections.title: Make one important account boring to attack.
points: Open the security page of your primary email provider from a trusted device.
Review recent activity, recovery addresses, phone numbers, and signed-in devices.
Add a passkey and complete one test sign-in with it.
Save recovery codes offline and record where the passkey is stored.
Set a calendar reminder to review access again in six months.
paragraphs: The goal is not a future with no responsibility. It is a future where the strongest behaviour is also the easiest normal behaviour. Passkeys remove one of the most exploitable human tasks, while careful recovery and device hygiene keep the whole system honest.
